prompt: In an Argo CD `Application` manifest, which field tells the controller which cluster and namespace the rendered manifests should be deployed into?
optionNotes: `spec.destination` holds `server` (or `name`) and `namespace`, identifying the target cluster and namespace, so it is the correct answer.
`spec.source` points at where the manifests come from: the Git/Helm repo URL, `targetRevision`, and `path` or `chart`.
`spec.project` names the `AppProject` that scopes what repos and destinations the Application is allowed to use; it is not the destination itself.
`spec.syncPolicy` controls how syncing happens (automated, prune, selfHeal, syncOptions), not where the resources go.
explanation: An Argo CD `Application` is essentially a mapping from a source (repo, revision, path) to a destination (cluster server/name plus namespace). `spec.destination` is where you put the target cluster and namespace. `spec.source` describes the origin, `spec.project` links to an `AppProject`, and `spec.syncPolicy` configures sync behaviour.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: guestbook
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/argoproj/argocd-example-apps.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: guestbook
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc   # in-cluster
    namespace: guestbook
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Git repo path guestbook"] -->|"spec.source"| A["Application CR"]
    A -->|"spec.destination"| C["Cluster https://kubernetes.default.svc"]
    C --> N["Namespace guestbook"]
    P["AppProject default"] -->|"spec.project scopes"| A

prompt: Which settings are valid child fields of `spec.syncPolicy.automated` in an Argo CD `Application`? (Select all that apply.)
optionNotes: `prune: true` lets an automated sync delete cluster resources whose manifests were removed from Git; it defaults to false for safety.
`selfHeal: true` makes Argo CD re-sync when live state drifts from Git even without a new commit; it is a valid `automated` field.
`allowEmpty: true` permits an automated sync that would result in zero resources, which is otherwise blocked as a guard against accidental wipe-outs.
`CreateNamespace=true` is a sync option that lives under `spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions`, not under `automated`.
`retry` is a sibling of `automated` under `spec.syncPolicy` (with `limit` and `backoff`), not a child of it.
There is no `hardRefresh` field; a hard refresh is an action triggered via the CLI/UI or the `argocd.argoproj.io/refresh: hard` annotation.
explanation: `spec.syncPolicy.automated` accepts `prune`, `selfHeal`, and `allowEmpty`. Prune and self-heal both default to false because they cause destructive or unrequested changes. `CreateNamespace=true` belongs in `syncOptions`, `retry` sits next to `automated`, and hard refresh is an operation, not a policy field.
example:
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true       # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true    # revert manual drift
      allowEmpty: false # refuse to sync to nothing
    syncOptions:
    - CreateNamespace=true
    retry:
      limit: 3
diagram:
flowchart TD
    S["spec.syncPolicy"] --> A["automated"]
    S --> O["syncOptions e.g. CreateNamespace=true"]
    S --> R["retry limit and backoff"]
    A --> P["prune"]
    A --> H["selfHeal"]
    A --> E["allowEmpty"]

prompt: Give the full annotation key you add to a Kubernetes manifest so that Argo CD applies it in a specific ordered phase (for example, a CRD before the resources that use it).
explanation: Sync waves are set with the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation whose value is an integer; lower waves are applied first and Argo CD waits for each wave to be healthy before moving on. Resources without the annotation are in wave 0. This is separate from hooks (`argocd.argoproj.io/hook`), which choose the phase (PreSync, Sync, PostSync).
example:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: widgets.example.com
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"   # applied before wave 0
---
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Widget
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"    # applied after the CRD is healthy
diagram:
flowchart LR
    W0["wave -1 CRD and Namespace"] -->|"healthy"| W1["wave 0 Deployment and Service"]
    W1 -->|"healthy"| W2["wave 1 custom resources"]
    W2 -->|"healthy"| W3["wave 2 smoke test Job"]

prompt: You need a Kubernetes `Job` that runs database schema migrations before Argo CD applies the new version of your Deployment, and you want the Job deleted once it succeeds. Which hook annotations achieve this?
optionNotes: `PreSync` runs before the main sync phase, and `HookSucceeded` removes the hook resource after it completes successfully, which is exactly the migration-then-cleanup requirement.

`PostSync` runs after all Sync-phase resources are healthy, so the migration would run after the new Deployment rolled out; `BeforeHookCreation` only deletes the old hook when the next one is about to be created.
A `Sync` hook runs during the main phase; sync waves order resources within a phase but the Job would still be part of the same phase as the Deployment and would not be cleaned up automatically.
`SyncFail` hooks only run when the sync operation fails, making them suitable for cleanup or notifications, not for a migration that must precede the rollout.
explanation: Argo CD resource hooks run at defined points of a sync: `PreSync` before manifests are applied, `Sync` alongside them, `PostSync` after everything is healthy, and `SyncFail` on failure. Pairing `PreSync` with `hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded` runs the migration first and garbage-collects the Job on success. The other combinations either run too late or only on failure.
example:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  generateName: db-migrate-
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: registry.example.com/app:1.4.0
        command: ["./migrate", "up"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["argocd app sync"] --> P["PreSync hook db-migrate Job"]
    P -->|"succeeded then deleted"| M["Sync phase apply Deployment"]
    M -->|"healthy"| Q["PostSync hook e.g. smoke test"]
    M -->|"error"| F["SyncFail hook"]

prompt: An Argo CD Application can report sync status `Synced` and health status `Degraded` at the same time.
explanation: Sync status and health status are independent. Sync status compares the desired manifests in Git with the live resources (`Synced` or `OutOfSync`), while health status is derived from the live objects themselves (`Healthy`, `Progressing`, `Degraded`, `Suspended`, `Missing`, `Unknown`). A Deployment whose Pods are crash-looping matches Git exactly but is `Degraded`.
example:
$ argocd app get guestbook
Name:          argocd/guestbook
Sync Status:   Synced to HEAD (a1b2c3d)
Health Status: Degraded   # Pods CrashLoopBackOff, manifests still match Git
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Manifests in Git"] -->|"diff"| SS["Sync status Synced or OutOfSync"]
    L["Live resources"] -->|"diff"| SS
    L -->|"resource conditions"| HS["Health status Healthy Progressing Degraded"]
    SS --> UI["Application card"]
    HS --> UI

prompt: Your monorepo has one directory per microservice under `apps/`, and you want Argo CD to create one `Application` for every directory automatically, picking up new directories as they are committed. Which `ApplicationSet` generator fits best?
optionNotes: The Git generator in directory mode scans a repo path pattern such as `apps/*` and emits one Application per matching directory, so newly committed directories appear automatically.
The List generator uses a static list of key/value elements written into the ApplicationSet itself; you would have to edit it each time a service is added.
The Cluster generator produces one Application per cluster registered in Argo CD, which is for fan-out across clusters rather than across directories.
The Pull Request generator creates ephemeral Applications for open pull requests from an SCM provider, which targets preview environments, not the set of services in a repo.
explanation: ApplicationSet generators produce parameter sets that are templated into Applications. The Git directory generator walks the repository at a path glob and yields `{{path}}` and `{{path.basename}}` for each directory, which is the standard way to bootstrap one Application per service in a monorepo. List, Cluster, and Pull Request generators solve different fan-out problems.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: services
spec:
  generators:
  - git:
      repoURL: https://github.com/example/platform.git
      revision: main
      directories:
      - path: apps/*
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{path.basename}}'
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/example/platform.git
        path: '{{path}}'
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["repo apps/*"] --> G["Git directory generator"]
    G --> P1["path apps/api"]
    G --> P2["path apps/web"]
    G --> P3["path apps/worker"]
    P1 --> A1["Application api"]
    P2 --> A2["Application web"]
    P3 --> A3["Application worker"]

prompt: An Argo CD Application still shows `OutOfSync` after you pushed a fix, and you suspect the controller is serving stale rendered manifests from the repo-server cache rather than re-rendering. What is the correct way to force Argo CD to discard cached manifests and regenerate them?
options: Wait for the next automatic reconciliation, which always re-renders manifests
optionNotes: A hard refresh (`--hard-refresh` on `app get`, or the `argocd.argoproj.io/refresh: hard` annotation) invalidates the repo-server manifest cache and re-renders from the commit, which is what is needed here.
`argocd app sync` applies whatever manifests Argo CD currently believes are desired; if those are cached and stale, syncing does not fix the underlying cache problem.
`argocd app diff` shows the difference between live and desired state using the same cached manifests, so it reports the problem but does not clear it.
A normal (soft) refresh, which the default 3-minute reconciliation performs, checks for a new commit but reuses cached manifests for the same commit and parameters, so it may not re-render.
explanation: Argo CD distinguishes a refresh (compare the latest Git commit against live state, reusing cached rendered manifests) from a hard refresh (also invalidate the manifest cache and re-run Helm/Kustomize/plugin rendering). Stale cache issues, for example after a Helm dependency or plugin change, require the hard variant. Sync and diff operate on the already-rendered desired state.
example:
# soft refresh: check for new commit, reuse cached manifests
argocd app get guestbook --refresh
# hard refresh: drop the repo-server cache and re-render
argocd app get guestbook --hard-refresh
# declarative equivalent
kubectl -n argocd annotate application guestbook argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=hard
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["argocd app get --hard-refresh"] --> C["application-controller"]
    C -->|"invalidate cache"| RS["repo-server"]
    RS -->|"clone and render Helm or Kustomize"| M["fresh manifests"]
    M --> D["compare with live state"]
    S["soft refresh"] -->|"reuses cached manifests"| D

prompt: A `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` keeps changing `spec.replicas` on a Deployment that Argo CD manages, so the Application flips to `OutOfSync` and self-heal fights the autoscaler. What is the recommended fix inside the `Application` spec?
options: Add an `ignoreDifferences` entry for the Deployment with `jsonPointers: [/spec/replicas]`
Add the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"` annotation to the Deployment
optionNotes: `ignoreDifferences` tells Argo CD to exclude the given JSON pointers (or JQ path expressions) from the diff, so HPA-driven replica changes no longer count as drift; this is the documented solution.
`prune` controls whether resources removed from Git are deleted; it has nothing to do with field-level diffs on an existing resource.
Sync waves control ordering during a sync and do not affect how the diff is computed.
`ApplyOutOfSyncOnly` makes syncs apply only resources that are out of sync; the Deployment would still be considered out of sync and self-heal would still overwrite replicas.
explanation: When another controller legitimately mutates a field, `spec.ignoreDifferences` lets you exclude that field from Argo CD's comparison, using `jsonPointers`, `jqPathExpressions`, or `managedFieldsManagers`. Combining it with the `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` sync option also keeps syncs from overwriting the field. Prune, waves, and `ApplyOutOfSyncOnly` do not change what counts as a difference.
example:
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
  - group: apps
    kind: Deployment
    jsonPointers:
    - /spec/replicas          # let the HPA own this field
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
    - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true   # do not overwrite it on sync
diagram:
flowchart LR
    H["HPA"] -->|"sets replicas 5"| D["Deployment live"]
    G["Git replicas 2"] --> C["Argo CD diff"]
    D --> C
    I["ignoreDifferences /spec/replicas"] -->|"mask field"| C
    C --> S["Synced no self-heal fight"]

prompt: In Argo Workflows, which template type lets you declare tasks with explicit `dependencies` so that independent tasks run in parallel and dependent ones wait for their predecessors?
optionNotes: A `dag` template lists `tasks`, each optionally naming `dependencies` (or a `depends` expression); the controller schedules the graph so unrelated tasks run concurrently, which is the described behaviour.
A `steps` template is a list of lists: the outer list runs sequentially and each inner list runs in parallel, giving ordering by position rather than by declared dependencies.
A `container` template is a leaf that runs a single container image; it does not orchestrate other templates.
A `suspend` template pauses the workflow until it is resumed manually or after a duration; it is not a way to compose tasks.
explanation: Argo Workflows offers two ways to orchestrate templates: `steps` (sequential outer list, parallel inner lists) and `dag` (a graph of tasks whose ordering comes from `dependencies`). DAGs are usually preferred for complex fan-out/fan-in because they express only real dependencies. `container` and `suspend` are leaf template types.
example:
templates:
- name: pipeline
  dag:
    tasks:
    - name: build
      template: build
    - name: unit-test
      template: test
      dependencies: [build]
    - name: lint
      template: lint
      dependencies: [build]     # runs in parallel with unit-test
    - name: deploy
      template: deploy
      dependencies: [unit-test, lint]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    B["build"] --> T["unit-test"]
    B --> L["lint"]
    T --> D["deploy"]
    L --> D

prompt: In Argo Workflows, a `WorkflowTemplate` is itself executed on a schedule by the workflow controller, whereas a `Workflow` is only a one-off manual run.
explanation: A `WorkflowTemplate` is a reusable, namespaced library of templates that does nothing on its own; it is invoked by a `Workflow` via `workflowTemplateRef` or `templateRef`, or submitted with `argo submit --from workflowtemplate/<name>`. Scheduled execution is the job of the separate `CronWorkflow` resource. A `Workflow` is the actual execution, whether created manually, by a CronWorkflow, or by an Argo Events sensor.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  generateName: nightly-etl-
spec:
  workflowTemplateRef:
    name: etl-template     # reuse the WorkflowTemplate
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: date
      value: "2026-09-11"
# schedule it instead with kind: CronWorkflow and spec.schedule
diagram:
flowchart LR
    WT["WorkflowTemplate reusable definition"]
    CW["CronWorkflow schedule"] -->|"creates"| W["Workflow execution"]
    M["argo submit --from"] -->|"creates"| W
    W -->|"workflowTemplateRef"| WT
    W --> P["Pods run steps"]

prompt: An Argo Rollouts canary strategy has the steps `setWeight: 20`, `pause: {}`, `setWeight: 60`, `pause: {duration: 10m}`, then full promotion. After the new ReplicaSet reaches 20% of traffic, what happens next?
options: The rollout pauses indefinitely at 20% until someone runs `kubectl argo rollouts promote` (or an analysis or UI action promotes it)
The rollout waits 10 minutes at 20% and then automatically moves to 60%
The rollout immediately shifts to 60% because an empty `pause` is a no-op
The rollout aborts because a `pause` without a duration is invalid
optionNotes: `pause: {}` with no `duration` is an indefinite pause; the Rollout status becomes Paused and it only continues when explicitly promoted, so this is correct.
A timed wait only happens for the second pause, which has `duration: 10m`; the first pause has no duration and therefore never expires on its own.
An empty pause is the opposite of a no-op; it is the standard way to insert a manual approval gate into a canary.
`pause: {}` is valid syntax documented for canary steps; no validation error occurs.
explanation: Canary steps run in order. `setWeight` shifts the traffic percentage (via replica ratios or a traffic router), and `pause` halts progress: without `duration` it is a manual gate cleared by `kubectl argo rollouts promote`, with `duration` it resumes automatically after the wait. This lets you combine a human check at 20% with an automatic soak at 60%, optionally backed by an `AnalysisTemplate` that can abort the rollout.
example:
strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
    - setWeight: 20
    - pause: {}                 # manual gate: kubectl argo rollouts promote app
    - setWeight: 60
    - pause: {duration: 10m}    # automatic soak
    analysis:
      templates:
      - templateName: success-rate   # AnalysisTemplate can abort on bad metrics
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["setWeight 20"] --> B["pause indefinite"]
    B -->|"promote"| C["setWeight 60"]
    C --> D["pause 10m"]
    D -->|"timer"| E["setWeight 100 promoted"]
    AN["AnalysisTemplate success-rate"] -->|"failed metric aborts"| R["rollback to stable"]

prompt: In Argo Events, an `EventSource` publishes events onto the `EventBus`. Name the resource kind that subscribes to those events, declares dependencies, and fires triggers such as creating a `Workflow`.
explanation: Argo Events has three main resources: the `EventBus` (transport, NATS or JetStream or Kafka), `EventSource` objects that ingest events from webhooks, queues, calendars, and so on, and `Sensor` objects that listen for one or more event dependencies and run triggers. Triggers commonly create Argo Workflows or arbitrary Kubernetes objects, or call HTTP endpoints.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Sensor
metadata:
  name: on-push
spec:
  dependencies:
  - name: gh
    eventSourceName: github
    eventName: push
  triggers:
  - template:
      name: run-ci
      argoWorkflow:
        operation: submit
        source:
          resource: { apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1, kind: Workflow }
diagram:
flowchart LR
    GH["GitHub webhook"] --> ES["EventSource github"]
    ES -->|"publish"| EB["EventBus"]
    EB -->|"subscribe"| SN["Sensor on-push"]
    SN -->|"trigger"| WF["Workflow submitted"]

prompt: Which statements are among the four OpenGitOps principles (v1.0.0)? (Select all that apply.)
options: The desired state of a system is expressed declaratively
Desired state is stored in a way that is versioned and immutable
Software agents automatically pull the desired state from the source
Software agents continuously observe actual state and attempt to apply the desired state
Changes are deployed by a CI pipeline pushing manifests with `kubectl apply`
Every change must be approved manually before it is reconciled
optionNotes: Principle 1, Declarative: the system's desired state is described as data, not as imperative steps.
Principle 2, Versioned and Immutable: desired state is kept in a store (typically Git) with a complete version history where versions are not mutated in place.
Principle 3, Pulled Automatically: agents fetch desired state from the store themselves rather than having it pushed to them.
Principle 4, Continuously Reconciled: agents keep comparing actual to desired state and correct differences, not just when a commit lands.
Push-based CI deployments contradict the pull principle; they are the traditional CI/CD model that GitOps replaces.
Manual approval is a process choice some teams add via pull requests, but it is not one of the principles and reconciliation itself is automatic.
explanation: The OpenGitOps project defines exactly four principles: Declarative, Versioned and Immutable, Pulled Automatically, and Continuously Reconciled. Pipeline-driven pushes and mandatory manual gates are not principles; the first violates automatic pull and the second describes an optional workflow around Git, not the reconciliation model.
example:
# principles in practice with Flux
flux create source git app --url=https://github.com/example/config --branch=main   # versioned, immutable store
flux create kustomization app --source=GitRepository/app --path=./prod --interval=1m # pulled automatically, continuously reconciled
# ./prod contains declarative YAML only
diagram:
flowchart TD
    O["OpenGitOps principles"] --> P1["1 Declarative"]
    O --> P2["2 Versioned and immutable"]
    O --> P3["3 Pulled automatically"]
    O --> P4["4 Continuously reconciled"]
    P2 --> G["Git as source of truth"]
    P3 --> A["agent in cluster fetches"]
    P4 --> A

prompt: What is the key difference between a pull-based GitOps deployment and a traditional push-based CI/CD deployment?
options: In pull-based GitOps an agent inside the target environment fetches desired state from Git; in push-based CI/CD the pipeline connects to the cluster and applies changes
Pull-based GitOps requires Kubernetes, whereas push-based CI/CD works with any platform
Pull-based GitOps stores manifests in the cluster, whereas push-based CI/CD stores them in Git
Pull-based GitOps needs cluster credentials in the CI system, whereas push-based CI/CD does not
optionNotes: This is the defining distinction: the reconciler (Argo CD, Flux) runs next to the workload and pulls from the repo, so the CI system never needs write access to production.
GitOps is most common on Kubernetes but the principles apply to any platform with a declarative API; the pull/push distinction is about direction, not platform.
Both models keep the source of truth in Git; what differs is who applies it and from where.
This is backwards: push-based pipelines are the ones that need cluster credentials, and removing that need is a major security benefit of the pull model.
explanation: In the push model a pipeline runner holds cluster credentials and runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade` when a build finishes. In the pull model an in-cluster agent polls or watches the repository and applies changes itself, and keeps reconciling afterwards. This reduces the credential blast radius, works through firewalls, and enables continuous drift correction.
example:
# push: CI job with cluster credentials
- run: kubectl --kubeconfig=$PROD_KUBECONFIG apply -k overlays/prod

# pull: agent inside the cluster, CI only commits
argocd app create api --repo https://github.com/example/config \
  --path overlays/prod --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Push
        CI["CI pipeline holds kubeconfig"] -->|"kubectl apply"| K1["Cluster"]
    end
    subgraph Pull
        G["Git repo"] -->|"fetch"| AG["Agent in cluster"]
        AG -->|"apply and reconcile"| K2["Cluster"]
    end

prompt: Under the Continuously Reconciled principle, a GitOps agent only needs to act when a new commit arrives in the repository; between commits the cluster is assumed to match Git.
explanation: Continuous reconciliation means the agent keeps observing actual state and comparing it to desired state on an ongoing loop, regardless of whether Git changed. Drift can originate from the cluster side, such as a manual `kubectl edit`, a crashed controller, or a deleted resource, and the reconciler is expected to detect and correct it. Reacting only to commits is event-driven delivery, not reconciliation.
example:
# Flux reconciles every interval even with no new commit
flux create kustomization app --source=GitRepository/app --path=./prod --interval=5m --prune
# manual drift is reverted on the next loop
kubectl scale deploy api --replicas=10   # reverted to Git value within 5m
diagram:
flowchart LR
    D["Desired state in Git"] --> C["Compare"]
    A["Actual state in cluster"] --> C
    C -->|"equal"| W["Wait interval"]
    C -->|"drift"| F["Apply desired state"]
    F --> W
    W --> C

prompt: An on-call engineer runs `kubectl set image deployment/api api=api:hotfix` in production. Ten minutes later the image is back to the version in Git. Which GitOps capability caused this, and what should the engineer have done instead?
options: Drift detection with self-healing reverted the change; the hotfix should have been committed to the config repository
The image pull policy re-pulled the old tag; the engineer should have used `imagePullPolicy: Always`
Garbage collection pruned the Deployment; the engineer should have disabled pruning
The CI pipeline re-ran on a timer and pushed the old image; the engineer should have paused CI
optionNotes: The reconciler compared live state to Git, saw the image field differ, and re-applied the declared version; in GitOps the fix is to change Git, which then flows to the cluster and is recorded.
Pull policy affects whether the kubelet re-downloads an image with the same tag; it never rewrites the Deployment's image field to a different tag.
Pruning deletes resources that are absent from Git; the Deployment still exists in Git, so it was corrected, not deleted.
In a pull-based model CI does not apply to the cluster at all, so a pipeline run cannot explain the revert.
explanation: Drift detection is the reconciler noticing that actual state diverges from desired state; self-healing (Argo CD `selfHeal`, Flux's default behaviour) is the automatic correction. Imperative changes made directly on the cluster are treated as drift and undone. The correct emergency path is a fast commit or a revert in Git so the change is versioned and auditable.
example:
# manual change is drift and gets reverted
kubectl set image deployment/api api=registry.example.com/api:hotfix

# GitOps way: change the source of truth
sed -i 's|api:1.4.0|api:hotfix|' overlays/prod/deployment.yaml
git commit -am "Hotfix api image in prod" && git push
diagram:
flowchart LR
    E["kubectl set image hotfix"] --> L["Live Deployment"]
    G["Git image 1.4.0"] --> R["Reconciler diff"]
    L --> R
    R -->|"drift detected selfHeal"| L
    E2["git commit hotfix"] --> G

prompt: A team models `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` as long-lived Git branches of the same config repository and promotes by merging `staging` into `prod`. Why is a directory-per-environment layout on a single branch generally recommended instead?
options: Environment branches drift apart over time because environment-specific commits (hotfixes, scaling tweaks) make merges conflict-prone and turn promotion into cherry-picking, whereas directories keep one history with explicit per-environment overlays
Git reconcilers such as Argo CD and Flux can only track the default branch of a repository
Directories let every environment share exactly the same manifests, so no per-environment differences are possible
Branch-based layouts prevent the use of Kustomize overlays or Helm values files
optionNotes: This is the core argument: branches are meant for converging work, but environments never converge, so their branches diverge permanently and promotions become error-prone merges; directories (with overlays) give one linear history and a diff-able promotion.
Both tools track any branch or tag (`targetRevision`, `spec.ref.branch`); the recommendation is about maintainability, not tool limitations.
The opposite is true: directories usually hold per-environment overlays or values files precisely to express differences; the base is shared, the overlay is not.
Overlays and values files work on any branch; the problem with branches is divergence and merge semantics, not tooling compatibility.
explanation: Git branches are designed to be merged back together, but environments are meant to stay different, so environment branches accumulate permanent divergence and promotions degrade into cherry-picks and conflict resolution. A single branch with `base/` plus `overlays/dev`, `overlays/staging`, `overlays/prod` keeps a single linear history where a promotion is an ordinary commit that changes one directory. Reconcilers support any branch, so the argument is about operability, not capability.
example:
config-repo/
  base/
    deployment.yaml
    kustomization.yaml
  overlays/
    dev/kustomization.yaml       # image tag, replicas for dev
    staging/kustomization.yaml
    prod/kustomization.yaml
# promotion = one commit changing overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Branches
        B1["dev branch"] -->|"merge conflicts"| B2["staging branch"]
        B2 -->|"cherry-pick"| B3["prod branch"]
    end
    subgraph Directories
        M["main branch"] --> D1["overlays/dev"]
        M --> D2["overlays/staging"]
        M --> D3["overlays/prod"]
    end

prompt: Which approaches let you safely commit secret material to a public-readable Git repository in encrypted form so that it can be decrypted inside the cluster? (Select all that apply.)
options: Mozilla SOPS with a KMS or age key, decrypted by the reconciler (for example Flux `decryption.provider: sops`)
Bitnami Sealed Secrets, where `kubeseal` encrypts with the controller's public key and the controller creates the `Secret`
External Secrets Operator syncing values from a vault into `Secret` objects
Committing a standard `Secret` manifest, since `data` values are base64-encoded
Storing secrets in a `ConfigMap` with restricted RBAC
optionNotes: SOPS encrypts the values of YAML/JSON files with keys from KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, PGP, or age; Flux and Argo CD plugins decrypt at reconcile time, so ciphertext is what lands in Git.
`kubeseal` produces a `SealedSecret` CR that only the in-cluster controller can decrypt with its private key; the CR is safe to commit and the controller materialises the real `Secret`.

External Secrets Operator does not put encrypted data in Git at all; the repo only contains an `ExternalSecret` reference and the value stays in the external store, so it is a valid pattern but not one that commits encrypted material.
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption; anyone who can read the repo can decode the value.
ConfigMaps are plaintext and not designed for secrets; RBAC on the cluster does nothing to protect data that is already in Git.
explanation: SOPS and Sealed Secrets both encrypt secret values before commit and rely on in-cluster decryption, making Git a safe store for them. External Secrets Operator solves the problem differently by keeping the value out of Git entirely and pulling it from a secret manager at runtime. Base64 and ConfigMaps provide no confidentiality.
example:
# SOPS: encrypt only the data/stringData fields
sops --encrypt --age $AGE_PUBLIC_KEY --encrypted-regex '^(data|stringData)$' secret.yaml > secret.enc.yaml

# Sealed Secrets: encrypt with the controller public key
kubeseal --format yaml < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml
git add secret.enc.yaml sealed-secret.yaml
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["plain Secret on laptop"] -->|"sops or kubeseal"| E["encrypted file"]
    E --> G["Git repo"]
    G --> R["reconciler or controller"]
    R -->|"decrypt with private key"| K["Secret in cluster"]
    V["Vault"] -->|"ESO fetches at runtime"| K

prompt: A deployment introduced by commit `f3a9c1` is causing errors. Which Git subcommand creates a new commit that undoes `f3a9c1` while preserving history, so the GitOps reconciler rolls the cluster back?
explanation: `git revert <commit>` adds a new commit whose changes are the inverse of the target, keeping history immutable and auditable, which is exactly what the Versioned and Immutable principle asks for. The reconciler sees the new HEAD and reconciles the cluster back to the previous state. `git reset --hard` plus a force push would rewrite history, and `kubectl rollout undo` would change the cluster without changing Git, so the agent would re-apply the bad version.
example:
git revert f3a9c1            # new commit inverting the bad change
git push origin main         # reconciler picks up the new HEAD
argocd app get api --refresh # or wait for the Flux interval
# avoid: git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git push --force  (rewrites history)
# avoid: kubectl rollout undo deployment/api          (drift, will be reverted)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C1["commit e1 good"] --> C2["commit f3a9c1 bad"]
    C2 --> C3["commit revert f3a9c1"]
    C3 --> R["reconciler applies"]
    R --> K["cluster back to good state"]
    X["kubectl rollout undo"] -.->|"drift reverted"| K

prompt: In Argo CD a single `Application` resource declares both where manifests come from and where they are deployed. Which pair of Flux resources together provides the equivalent for a Kustomize-based deployment from Git?
optionNotes: Flux separates fetching from applying: the `GitRepository` source object pulls and verifies the repo, and the `Kustomization` object points at a path in that source and applies it with pruning and health checks, which together match an Argo CD Application.
`HelmRepository` plus `HelmRelease` is the equivalent pair for Helm charts, not for a Kustomize directory in Git.
`ImageRepository` and `ImagePolicy` belong to Flux's image automation stack; they scan registries and pick tags, they do not deploy manifests.
`Bucket` is an S3-style source and `Receiver` is a webhook endpoint from notification-controller; neither applies manifests.
explanation: Argo CD bundles source and destination into one `Application`, while Flux uses a composable model: source-controller manages `GitRepository`, `OCIRepository`, `HelmRepository`, and `Bucket` objects, and kustomize-controller or helm-controller consume them via `Kustomization` or `HelmRelease`. Knowing the mapping helps when comparing the two tools or migrating between them. The image and notification resources handle automation and events, not deployment.
example:
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata: { name: app, namespace: flux-system }
spec:
  url: https://github.com/example/config
  ref: { branch: main }
  interval: 1m
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata: { name: app, namespace: flux-system }
spec:
  sourceRef: { kind: GitRepository, name: app }
  path: ./overlays/prod
  prune: true
  interval: 5m
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph ArgoCD
        AP["Application source plus destination"]
    end
    subgraph Flux
        GR["GitRepository fetch repo"] --> KS["Kustomization apply path"]
        KS --> C["Cluster"]
    end
    AP -.->|"equivalent to"| GR

prompt: GitOps requires that application source code and the Kubernetes deployment manifests for that application live in the same Git repository.
explanation: GitOps only requires that desired state be declarative and stored in a versioned, immutable source; it does not dictate repository layout. The common recommendation is actually the opposite: keep a separate config repository so that a CI build does not trigger a deployment loop, deployment history is not polluted by code commits, and access can be granted to operators without exposing application source. Monorepos are still a valid choice for small teams.
example:
# separate repos: CI updates config repo, reconciler watches only config repo
app-repo/      src/, Dockerfile, .github/workflows/build.yml
config-repo/   base/, overlays/prod/   <-- Argo CD or Flux points here

# CI step in app-repo
kustomize edit set image api=registry.example.com/api:$GIT_SHA   # run inside a clone of config-repo
git commit -am "Deploy api $GIT_SHA" && git push
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["app repo source code"] -->|"CI builds image"| REG["registry"]
    A -->|"CI commits new tag"| C["config repo manifests"]
    C -->|"pull"| R["reconciler"]
    REG --> K["cluster"]
    R --> K

prompt: A platform team wants each production release to reach 10% of users first, be judged automatically against error-rate and latency metrics from Prometheus, and roll back without human involvement if the metrics regress. Which practice is being described?
options: Blue-green deployment with a manual switch
optionNotes: Progressive delivery gradually exposes a new version to a growing share of traffic while automated analysis (Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate`, Flagger metric checks) gates or reverts the rollout; this matches every element of the scenario.
Blue-green runs two full environments and flips all traffic at once; it can be automated but does not involve partial traffic percentages or gradual exposure.
Recreate stops the old version before starting the new one, with downtime and no traffic splitting.
Branching and promotion concern how changes move through Git and environments, not how traffic is shifted or measured in production.
explanation: Progressive delivery extends continuous delivery with controlled rollout of a change, typically canary traffic shifting, plus automated metric analysis that promotes or aborts the release. In a GitOps setup the desired state in Git still says "version 2", but a controller such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger manages how quickly the cluster converges to it. Blue-green and recreate are all-at-once strategies.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: { name: success-rate }
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: success-rate
    interval: 1m
    successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99
    failureLimit: 2          # abort and roll back after 2 failures
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api",code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api"}[5m]))
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Git version 2"] --> RC["rollout controller"]
    RC -->|"10 percent"| CN["canary pods"]
    RC -->|"90 percent"| ST["stable pods"]
    PM["Prometheus metrics"] --> AN["automated analysis"]
    AN -->|"pass"| PR["promote to 100 percent"]
    AN -->|"fail"| RB["automatic rollback"]

prompt: Flux image automation (`ImageRepository`, `ImagePolicy`, `ImageUpdateAutomation`) detects a new tag `api:1.5.0` in the registry. Why does it commit the new tag into the config repository rather than simply patching the Deployment in the cluster?
options: Because Git must remain the single source of truth: patching the cluster directly would be drift that the reconciler reverts, and the change would be unversioned and unauditable
Because the Flux controllers do not have RBAC permission to modify Deployments
Because image tags can only be changed through a Kustomize `images` transformer, which is Git-only
Because the registry webhook can only deliver events to a Git provider
optionNotes: Writing the tag to Git keeps the Versioned and Immutable and Continuously Reconciled principles intact: the new version becomes a commit that the normal reconciliation loop applies, can be reviewed, and can be reverted with `git revert`.
Flux controllers run with cluster-admin-level permissions by default and kustomize-controller patches Deployments all the time; permissions are not the reason.
The automation uses `# {"$imagepolicy": ...}` markers and can update any YAML field, and Kustomize transformers are not the only way to set images.
Registry webhooks target Flux's notification-controller `Receiver` to speed up scans; they are unrelated to where the update is written.
explanation: Image update automation is a write-back pattern: the controller scans the registry, selects a tag by policy (semver range, alphabetical, numerical), then edits the marked fields in Git and pushes a commit. The cluster changes only because Git changed, so history, review, and rollback all keep working. Argo CD Image Updater with its `git` write-back method follows the same reasoning.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    REG["registry api 1.5.0"] --> IR["ImageRepository scan"]
    IR --> IP["ImagePolicy pick semver"]
    IP --> IUA["ImageUpdateAutomation"]
    IUA -->|"commit and push"| G["config repo"]
    G -->|"normal reconcile"| K["cluster Deployment 1.5.0"]

prompt: Which of these is a genuine limitation or challenge of adopting GitOps, rather than a benefit?
options: Imperative or one-off operational tasks (database migrations, ad-hoc restarts, ordering across systems) do not map cleanly onto declarative, continuously reconciled state
Every change to the environment is recorded as a commit with an author and timestamp
Cluster credentials no longer need to be distributed to CI systems
Disaster recovery can be performed by pointing a new cluster at the same repository
optionNotes: GitOps excels at desired state, but jobs that must run exactly once, in a specific order, or that depend on external systems require workarounds such as sync hooks, waves, Jobs with generated names, or separate workflow engines; this is a well-known limitation.
A complete, attributable audit trail is one of the primary benefits of GitOps.
Removing cluster write credentials from CI is a security benefit of the pull model.
Repeatable rebuilds from the repository are a resilience benefit, not a limitation.
explanation: GitOps brings auditability, reproducibility, and reduced credential sprawl, but it is a poor fit for imperative procedures and for state that lives outside the declarative model. Other common challenges include secret management, handling many environments and repositories at scale, and reconcilers overwriting changes made by other controllers. The three other options are textbook benefits.
example:
# workaround for a one-off task in Argo CD: a PreSync hook Job
metadata:
  generateName: migrate-      # new Job each sync
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded
# still not ideal: ordering across clusters, external approvals, manual runbooks
diagram:
flowchart TD
    G["GitOps"] --> B1["benefit audit trail"]
    G --> B2["benefit no CI cluster creds"]
    G --> B3["benefit rebuild from repo"]
    G --> L1["limitation imperative one-off tasks"]
    G --> L2["limitation secrets in Git"]
    G --> L3["limitation controller conflicts"]

prompt: You want a Kubernetes `Job` that posts an alert to Slack only when an Argo CD sync operation fails. Which value of the `argocd.argoproj.io/hook` annotation runs a resource in that situation?
optionNotes: `SyncFail` hooks run only when the sync operation fails, which is exactly the alerting case.
`PostSync` hooks run after a successful sync once all resources are healthy; they do not run on failure.
`Skip` tells Argo CD not to apply the resource at all; it is not a failure handler.
`OnFailure` is not an Argo CD hook phase; the recognised phases are PreSync, Sync, PostSync, SyncFail, PostDelete and Skip.
explanation: Argo CD resource hooks are selected with the `argocd.argoproj.io/hook` annotation. `SyncFail` hooks execute only when the sync operation fails, making them the right place for failure notifications or cleanup. `PostSync` runs only after success, and `Skip` suppresses applying the resource.
example:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: notify-sync-failed
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: SyncFail
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: notify
        image: curlimages/curl
        args: ["-X", "POST", "$(SLACK_WEBHOOK)", "-d", "{\"text\": \"sync failed\"}"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    PRE["PreSync hooks"] --> S["Sync phase apply manifests"]
    S -->|"success"| POST["PostSync hooks"]
    S -->|"failure"| F["SyncFail hooks e.g. Slack alert Job"]

prompt: Give the exact entry you add under `spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions` so that Argo CD applies manifests with Kubernetes server-side apply instead of client-side `kubectl apply`.
explanation: `ServerSideApply=true` switches the sync to server-side apply, which lets the API server own field management, avoids the 262KB `last-applied-configuration` annotation limit, and allows Argo CD to patch only the fields it manages. It can also be set per resource with the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: ServerSideApply=true` annotation.
example:
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
    - ServerSideApply=true
    - CreateNamespace=true
# or per resource:
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: ServerSideApply=true
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Manifest in Git"] --> A["Argo CD sync"]
    A -->|"default client-side apply"| C["kubectl apply with last-applied annotation"]
    A -->|"ServerSideApply=true"| S["API server field manager argocd-controller"]
    S --> L["Live object"]
    C --> L

prompt: An Argo CD sync of a large `CustomResourceDefinition` fails with `metadata.annotations: Too long: must have at most 262144 bytes`. Which sync option is the most targeted fix, and what trade-off does it carry?
options: `Replace=true` on that resource: Argo CD uses `kubectl replace` instead of apply, but the object is recreated on each sync and can lose fields set by other controllers
`Prune=false` on that resource: Argo CD stops deleting it, but it is still applied client-side
`Validate=false` on that resource: Argo CD skips schema validation, so the annotation size limit no longer applies
`PruneLast=true` at the Application level: the CRD is applied in a final wave where the annotation is not written
optionNotes: `Replace=true` sends the whole object with `replace`, which never writes the `last-applied-configuration` annotation; the cost is that replace overwrites fields other controllers may have set and can fail on immutable fields. `ServerSideApply=true` is the alternative that avoids the annotation as well.
`Prune=false` only affects deletion behaviour; the apply still writes the oversized annotation and fails.
`Validate=false` disables `kubectl --validate`, which is client-side schema validation. The annotation size limit is enforced by the API server regardless.
`PruneLast=true` changes when pruning happens, not how objects are applied, and does not affect the annotation.
explanation: The error comes from `kubectl apply` storing the full manifest in the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation, which has a 256KB limit. Setting `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Replace=true` on the resource makes Argo CD use `kubectl replace`, which skips that annotation. Because replace overwrites the entire object, `ServerSideApply=true` is usually the safer modern choice.
example:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: prometheuses.monitoring.coreos.com
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Replace=true
# alternative: ServerSideApply=true
diagram:
flowchart TD
    E["apply fails: annotation over 262144 bytes"] --> R["Replace=true kubectl replace"]
    E --> S["ServerSideApply=true field management"]
    R --> T["Trade-off: whole object overwritten, immutable fields may fail"]
    S --> U["Trade-off: field ownership conflicts to resolve"]

prompt: An Argo CD `Application` in project `team-a` shows the error `application repo https://github.com/acme/infra.git is not permitted in project 'team-a'`. Which `AppProject` field must be updated to fix this?
optionNotes: `spec.sourceRepos` lists the Git or Helm repository URLs (glob patterns allowed) an Application in this project may pull from; the error names exactly this restriction.
`spec.destinations` limits which cluster/namespace pairs the project may deploy to; a violation there produces a different error about the destination.
`spec.clusterResourceWhitelist` controls which cluster-scoped kinds (for example `Namespace` or `ClusterRole`) may be created, not which repositories are allowed.
`spec.roles` defines project-scoped RBAC roles and JWT tokens; it does not gate repository access.
explanation: An `AppProject` restricts Applications on three axes: `sourceRepos` (where manifests may come from), `destinations` (where they may be deployed) and resource whitelists/blacklists (what kinds may be created). The `not permitted in project` repo error is fixed by adding the URL or a matching glob to `spec.sourceRepos`.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: team-a
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  sourceRepos:
  - https://github.com/acme/infra.git
  - https://github.com/acme/team-a-*
  destinations:
  - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: team-a-*
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
  - group: ""
    kind: Namespace
diagram:
flowchart TD
    P["AppProject team-a"] --> SR["sourceRepos allowed repo URLs"]
    P --> DS["destinations allowed cluster and namespace"]
    P --> CW["clusterResourceWhitelist allowed cluster-scoped kinds"]
    A["Application repoURL acme/infra"] -->|"checked against"| SR

prompt: Which of the following are real generator types available in an Argo CD `ApplicationSet`? (Select all that apply.)
optionNotes: The `list` generator takes a static list of key/value elements and produces one Application per element.
The `cluster` generator produces one Application per cluster registered in Argo CD, optionally filtered by cluster secret labels.
The `pullRequest` generator creates an Application for each open pull request from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket and others, commonly used for preview environments.
The `matrix` generator combines two child generators, producing the cartesian product of their parameters (for example clusters times Git directories).
There is no `helm` generator; Helm is a source type inside the Application template, not a way to generate parameters.
There is no `namespace` generator; to fan out over namespaces you would use `list` or a Git files generator.
explanation: ApplicationSet generators supply parameters to a template. The built-in set is `list`, `cluster`, `git` (directories or files), `matrix`, `merge`, `scmProvider`, `pullRequest`, `clusterDecisionResource` and `plugin`. Helm and namespaces are not generators.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: previews
spec:
  generators:
  - pullRequest:
      github:
        owner: acme
        repo: web
        labels: [preview]
      requeueAfterSeconds: 60
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'web-pr-{{number}}'
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/acme/web.git
        targetRevision: '{{head_sha}}'
        path: deploy
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: 'pr-{{number}}'
      project: default
diagram:
flowchart LR
    L["list"] --> T["template"]
    C["cluster"] --> T
    G["git directories or files"] --> T
    PR["pullRequest"] --> T
    M["matrix combines two generators"] --> T
    T --> A1["Application 1"]
    T --> A2["Application N"]

prompt: A platform team bootstraps a new cluster by creating a single Argo CD `Application` whose source path contains only other `Application` manifests. What is this pattern called?
optionNotes: App of Apps is a parent Application that manages child Application resources in Git, letting one `argocd app create` bootstrap everything declaratively.
An `ApplicationSet` is a separate CRD that generates Applications from generators; it is often used instead of App of Apps but is not the name of this pattern.
A multi-source Application combines several `spec.sources` into one Application; it does not create other Applications.
Project bootstrap is not an Argo CD term; `AppProject` scopes permissions and does not create Applications.
explanation: In the App of Apps pattern the parent Application points at a directory of child `Application` manifests, so Argo CD applies them and then reconciles each child in turn. It is a common way to bootstrap a whole cluster from one root Application, and ApplicationSet is the newer, generator-driven alternative.
example:
# apps/root.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/children   # contains monitoring.yaml, ingress.yaml, ...
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {}
diagram:
flowchart TD
    R["root Application path apps/children"] --> M["Application monitoring"]
    R --> I["Application ingress"]
    R --> W["Application web"]
    M --> MK["kube-prometheus manifests"]
    I --> IK["ingress-nginx manifests"]
    W --> WK["web manifests"]

prompt: You want one Argo CD Application for every combination of registered cluster labelled `env=prod` and every directory under `addons/` in your Git repo. Which ApplicationSet construction achieves this?
options: A `matrix` generator whose two child generators are a `cluster` generator with a label selector and a `git` directories generator
A `merge` generator combining a `cluster` generator and a `git` generator on the key `name`
Two separate generators listed under `spec.generators`, one `cluster` and one `git`, which are automatically multiplied
A `cluster` generator with `directories` nested under it
optionNotes: `matrix` computes the cartesian product of two generators, so N clusters times M directories yields N times M Applications with both parameter sets available to the template.
`merge` joins parameter sets that share a merge key, overriding fields from the base set; it does not multiply them and the sets here share no common key.
Listing multiple generators concatenates their outputs (union), it does not combine them; you would get N cluster Applications plus M directory Applications, each missing the other's parameters.
The `cluster` generator has no `directories` field; directory discovery belongs to the `git` generator.
explanation: The `matrix` generator is specifically for cartesian products. Its `generators` list takes exactly two child generators, and the template can reference parameters from both, such as `{{.name}}` and `{{.server}}` from the cluster and `{{.path.basename}}` from the git directory. Multiple top-level generators are unioned, not multiplied.
example:
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  generators:
  - matrix:
      generators:
      - clusters:
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              env: prod
      - git:
          repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
          revision: main
          directories:
          - path: addons/*
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{.path.basename}}-{{.name}}'
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: '{{.path.path}}'
      destination:
        server: '{{.server}}'
        namespace: '{{.path.basename}}'
      project: default
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["clusters env=prod: eu, us"] --> M["matrix generator"]
    G["git directories: cert-manager, ingress"] --> M
    M --> A1["cert-manager-eu"]
    M --> A2["cert-manager-us"]
    M --> A3["ingress-eu"]
    M --> A4["ingress-us"]

prompt: Deleting an Argo CD `Application` resource always deletes the Kubernetes resources that the Application was managing.
explanation: Whether managed resources are removed depends on the finalizer. With `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` on the Application (the default when created with `argocd app create` or the UI cascade option), deletion cascades to the managed resources. Without the finalizer, or when you run `argocd app delete --cascade=false`, only the Application object is removed and the workloads stay in the cluster.
example:
# cascading delete: resources are removed in the foreground
metadata:
  finalizers:
  - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io

$ argocd app delete guestbook            # cascades if finalizer present
$ argocd app delete guestbook --cascade=false   # keep the workloads
diagram:
flowchart TD
    D["kubectl delete application guestbook"] --> Q["finalizer resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io present?"]
    Q -->|"yes"| C["controller deletes managed Deployments, Services..."]
    C --> R["finalizer removed, Application gone"]
    Q -->|"no"| O["only the Application object is removed, workloads remain"]

prompt: Which `argocd` CLI command prints the differences between the live resources in the cluster and the manifests rendered from Git for an application, exiting non-zero when there are differences? Give the command without the application name.
explanation: `argocd app diff <app>` renders the target manifests and compares them with the live state, printing a unified diff and returning exit code 1 when differences exist, which makes it useful in CI checks. Flags like `--revision` and `--local` let you diff against an arbitrary Git revision or a local directory before pushing.
example:
$ argocd app diff guestbook
===== apps/Deployment guestbook/guestbook-ui ======
@@ spec.replicas
-  1
+  3
$ echo $?
1
# diff a local checkout before committing
$ argocd app diff guestbook --local ./guestbook
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Git rendered manifests"] --> D["argocd app diff"]
    L["Live cluster objects"] --> D
    D -->|"no changes"| Z["exit 0"]
    D -->|"differences"| O["unified diff, exit 1"]

prompt: Which of the following are valid step types inside `spec.strategy.canary.steps` of an Argo Rollouts `Rollout`? (Select all that apply.)
optionNotes: `setWeight` shifts the given percentage of traffic (or replicas without a traffic router) to the canary ReplicaSet.
`pause` halts progression either indefinitely (until promoted) or for a `duration`.
`analysis` runs an inline `AnalysisRun` from an `AnalysisTemplate` at that step; the rollout aborts if it fails.
`setCanaryScale` decouples the canary replica count from the traffic weight when using a traffic router, using `replicas`, `weight` or `matchTrafficWeight`.
`promote` is not a step; promotion is done with `kubectl argo rollouts promote` or by finishing the last step.
`rollbackWindow` is a top-level `spec.rollbackWindow` field that allows fast rollback to recent revisions; it is not a canary step.
explanation: Canary steps are `setWeight`, `pause`, `analysis`, `experiment`, `setCanaryScale`, `setHeaderRoute`, `setMirrorRoute` and `plugin`. Promotion and rollback windows are operations or top-level fields rather than steps.
example:
strategy:
  canary:
    canaryService: web-canary
    stableService: web-stable
    trafficRouting:
      nginx:
        stableIngress: web
    steps:
    - setCanaryScale:
        weight: 50
    - setWeight: 10
    - pause: {duration: 5m}
    - analysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: error-rate
    - setWeight: 50
    - pause: {}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S1["setWeight 10"] --> S2["pause 5m"]
    S2 --> S3["analysis error-rate"]
    S3 -->|"pass"| S4["setWeight 50"]
    S3 -->|"fail"| AB["abort, traffic back to stable"]
    S4 --> S5["pause until promote"]
    S5 --> P["100 percent stable"]

prompt: An Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate` queries Prometheus every 30 seconds for the canary success ratio. You want the analysis to fail the rollout only if the ratio drops below 0.95 on three measurements, while a single bad sample should not abort. Which combination of fields expresses this?
optionNotes: A measurement that violates `successCondition` counts as a failure; `failureLimit: 2` tolerates two failed measurements and the third marks the analysis Failed, aborting the rollout. `interval` sets the 30 second cadence.
`count: 3` limits the analysis to three measurements in total and then finishes; with the default `failureLimit: 0` the first bad sample already fails the run.
`consecutiveErrorLimit` counts measurement errors such as Prometheus being unreachable, not measurements that returned a value below the threshold.
`inconclusiveLimit` applies to measurements that satisfy neither the success nor failure condition; a value below 0.95 with only a `successCondition` is a failure, not inconclusive.
explanation: In an `AnalysisTemplate` metric, each measurement is evaluated against `successCondition` (and optionally `failureCondition`). `failureLimit` is the number of failed measurements allowed before the whole analysis is marked Failed, so `failureLimit: 2` means the third failure aborts. `consecutiveErrorLimit` and `inconclusiveLimit` handle provider errors and ambiguous results respectively.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate
spec:
  args:
  - name: service
  metrics:
  - name: success-rate
    interval: 30s
    failureLimit: 2
    successCondition: result[0] >= 0.95
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service}}",code!~"5.."}[2m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service}}"}[2m]))
diagram:
flowchart LR
    M["measurement every 30s"] --> E["result 0 at least 0.95?"]
    E -->|"yes"| OK["Successful measurement"]
    E -->|"no"| F["failed count plus 1"]
    F -->|"failed count greater than failureLimit 2"| X["AnalysisRun Failed, rollout aborted"]
    F -->|"otherwise"| M

prompt: Which of the following are real `flux` CLI commands? (Select all that apply.)
optionNotes: `flux bootstrap github` installs the Flux controllers, commits their manifests to a repository and configures Flux to manage itself from that repo.
`flux reconcile kustomization <name>` triggers an immediate reconciliation instead of waiting for the next interval; `--with-source` also refreshes the source first.
`flux suspend helmrelease <name>` pauses reconciliation of that release, for example during an incident, and `flux resume` undoes it.
There is no `flux apply`; Flux applies manifests itself from sources and you commit changes to Git rather than applying with the CLI.
There is no `flux sync` command; the equivalent is `flux reconcile`.
`flux get sources git` lists `GitRepository` objects with their revision and readiness.
explanation: The `flux` CLI wraps bootstrap, installation, inspection (`get`, `logs`, `events`, `tree`), and control (`reconcile`, `suspend`, `resume`) of Flux resources. It intentionally has no `apply` because the desired state is meant to come from Git or OCI, not from an operator's terminal.
example:
$ flux bootstrap github --owner=acme --repository=fleet --path=clusters/prod --personal=false
$ flux get sources git
$ flux reconcile kustomization apps --with-source
$ flux suspend helmrelease ingress-nginx -n flux-system
$ flux resume helmrelease ingress-nginx -n flux-system
diagram:
flowchart LR
    B["flux bootstrap"] --> R["Flux controllers plus repo commit"]
    R --> G["flux get sources git"]
    R --> RC["flux reconcile kustomization"]
    R --> S["flux suspend helmrelease"]
    S --> RS["flux resume helmrelease"]

prompt: A Flux `HelmRelease` upgrade fails because a new chart version has a broken template. You want Flux to roll back to the previous release automatically and try the upgrade again a limited number of times. Which field configures this?
optionNotes: `spec.upgrade.remediation.retries: N` makes Flux remediate a failed upgrade (rollback by default, or uninstall with `strategy: uninstall`) and retry up to N times before giving up.
`spec.rollback` exists but only tunes how a rollback is performed (timeout, cleanupOnFail, force); it does not enable rollbacks by itself.
`spec.install.remediation` applies to the first install of a release, where the remediation is an uninstall, not to upgrades of an existing release.
`spec.upgrade.force` passes Helm's `--force` to recreate resources on upgrade; it does not add retries or rollbacks.
explanation: Flux's helm-controller separates install remediation (uninstall and retry) from upgrade remediation (rollback and retry). Setting `spec.upgrade.remediation.retries` to a positive number enables automatic rollback on failure with that many retries; `remediateLastFailure` controls whether the final failed attempt is also rolled back and defaults to true once retries is greater than zero.
example:
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: podinfo
  namespace: default
spec:
  interval: 10m
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: podinfo
      version: '6.x'
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: podinfo
  upgrade:
    remediation:
      retries: 3
      strategy: rollback
diagram:
flowchart TD
    U["helm upgrade"] -->|"fails"| R["remediation strategy rollback"]
    R --> C["retries remaining?"]
    C -->|"yes"| U
    C -->|"no"| F["HelmRelease Ready=False, stalled until spec changes"]
    U -->|"succeeds"| OK["Ready=True"]

prompt: A Flux `OCIRepository` source lets Flux pull Kubernetes manifests that were pushed to a container registry as an OCI artifact, so a cluster can be reconciled without any Git access.
explanation: `OCIRepository` (source-controller) fetches artifacts published with `flux push artifact` or other OCI tooling to registries such as GHCR, ECR or Harbor. A `Kustomization` or `HelmRelease` can reference it via `sourceRef.kind: OCIRepository`, which lets CI build and sign artifacts while clusters pull from the registry instead of Git.
example:
$ flux push artifact oci://ghcr.io/acme/manifests/podinfo:v1.2.0 --path=./deploy --source=$(git config --get remote.origin.url) --revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
---
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: OCIRepository
metadata:
  name: podinfo
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 5m
  url: oci://ghcr.io/acme/manifests/podinfo
  ref:
    tag: v1.2.0
  verify:
    provider: cosign
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Git commit"] --> CI["CI: flux push artifact"]
    CI --> R["OCI registry ghcr.io"]
    R -->|"pull artifact"| O["OCIRepository"]
    O --> K["Kustomization sourceRef OCIRepository"]
    K --> C["Cluster"]

prompt: In a Flux-managed cluster, a manual `kubectl edit` to a Deployment applied by a `Kustomization` is reverted within minutes, but the same edit to a Deployment installed by a `HelmRelease` persists indefinitely. What explains the difference?
options: Kustomization always corrects drift with server-side apply, while HelmRelease drift detection is off unless `spec.driftDetection.mode` is set to `enabled` or `warn`
HelmRelease only reconciles when the chart version changes, so drift can never be corrected for Helm releases
The HelmRelease is suspended; Flux suspends any release after a manual edit to protect operator changes
Kustomization uses `prune: true`, which deletes and recreates edited objects, whereas Helm has no prune
optionNotes: The kustomize-controller server-side applies every interval and therefore undoes drift. The helm-controller by default only compares the desired release (chart plus values) with the stored Helm release, not with live objects; `spec.driftDetection.mode: enabled` makes it diff and correct cluster state.
HelmRelease reconciles at `spec.interval` regardless of chart changes, but without drift detection it sees no difference in the Helm release and does nothing.
Flux never auto-suspends a resource; suspension is explicit via `spec.suspend: true` or `flux suspend`.
`prune` only removes objects that disappeared from the source; it has nothing to do with correcting field-level drift.
explanation: Drift correction differs between controllers. Kustomization reconciliation re-applies manifests via server-side apply every interval, so drift is undone. HelmRelease drift detection (helm-controller v0.37 and later, GA in `helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2`) must be turned on with `spec.driftDetection.mode: enabled`; `warn` only logs, and `ignore` rules can exclude fields such as replica counts managed by an HPA.
example:
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: podinfo
spec:
  interval: 10m
  driftDetection:
    mode: enabled
    ignore:
    - paths: ["/spec/replicas"]
      target:
        kind: Deployment
diagram:
flowchart TD
    E["manual kubectl edit"] --> K["Kustomization: server-side apply each interval"]
    K --> RV["drift reverted"]
    E --> H["HelmRelease default: compare desired vs stored release only"]
    H --> P["drift persists"]
    H -->|"driftDetection.mode enabled"| D["diff live objects and patch"]
    D --> RV

prompt: When using External Secrets Operator in a GitOps workflow, the actual secret values are stored encrypted inside the `ExternalSecret` manifests committed to Git.
explanation: `ExternalSecret` manifests contain only references: which `SecretStore` or `ClusterSecretStore` to use and which keys to read from the backend (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, GCP Secret Manager and so on). The operator fetches the values at runtime and writes a regular Kubernetes `Secret`, so nothing sensitive lives in Git. That is the main difference from SOPS or Sealed Secrets, which do commit encrypted ciphertext.
example:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets-manager
  target:
    name: db-creds   # Kubernetes Secret created by the operator
  data:
  - secretKey: password
    remoteRef:
      key: prod/db
      property: password   # value never appears in Git
diagram:
flowchart LR
    G["Git: ExternalSecret with references only"] --> A["Argo CD or Flux applies it"]
    A --> O["External Secrets Operator"]
    O -->|"fetch by key"| V["AWS Secrets Manager or Vault"]
    V --> O
    O --> S["Kubernetes Secret db-creds"]

prompt: Your Helm chart lives in `https://github.com/acme/charts.git` but the environment-specific `values-prod.yaml` lives in a separate `https://github.com/acme/config.git` repository. Which Argo CD feature lets a single Application render the chart with values from the second repo?
options: Multi-source Applications using `spec.sources` with a `ref` on the values repo and `$ref/path` in `helm.valueFiles`
A Kustomize `helmCharts` entry in the config repo pointing at the chart repo
`spec.source.helm.values` with a `git::` URL to the remote values file
An `ApplicationSet` with a `merge` generator joining the two repositories
optionNotes: With `spec.sources`, one source can declare `ref: values` and another can reference files from it as `$values/env/prod/values-prod.yaml` in `helm.valueFiles`, which is the documented way to split chart and values across repos.
Kustomize `helmCharts` renders charts from a Helm repository index, not from a Git repo, and it would move rendering to Kustomize rather than use Argo CD's Helm support.
`helm.values` accepts inline YAML only; Argo CD does not resolve remote `git::` URLs inside it.
ApplicationSet generators produce Application parameters; they do not make one Application read files from a second repository.
explanation: Multi-source Applications (GA since Argo CD 2.6 with continued improvements) let `spec.sources` list several sources. A source with only `repoURL` and `ref` contributes no manifests but exposes its files under `$<ref>/...` so that a Helm source can pull `valueFiles` from it.
example:
spec:
  sources:
  - repoURL: https://github.com/acme/charts.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: charts/api
    helm:
      valueFiles:
      - $values/env/prod/values-prod.yaml
  - repoURL: https://github.com/acme/config.git
    targetRevision: main
    ref: values
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["charts.git path charts/api"] --> A["Application spec.sources"]
    V["config.git ref values"] --> A
    A -->|"helm valueFiles $values/env/prod/values-prod.yaml"| R["rendered manifests"]
    R --> K["Cluster"]

prompt: Argo CD Image Updater is configured with `argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/image-list: api=ghcr.io/acme/api` and `argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/write-back-method: git`. When a new tag is detected, what does it do?
options: Commits an override file (for example `.argocd-source-<app>.yaml`) with the new image tag to the Application's Git repository, so Argo CD syncs it from Git
Patches the live Deployment in the cluster directly with the new image and marks the Application as `Synced`
Updates `spec.source.helm.parameters` on the `Application` resource in the cluster without touching Git
Opens a pull request that must be merged before the Application changes
optionNotes: With the `git` write-back method the updater commits the new tag to the tracked repository and branch (optionally a separate `git-branch`), preserving the Git-as-source-of-truth model and letting Argo CD deploy it through a normal sync.
Image Updater never modifies workloads directly; that would create drift that Argo CD would revert.
Updating the Application's parameters in-cluster is the `argocd` write-back method, which is simpler but leaves the actual tag outside Git.
Opening a pull request is not a built-in write-back method; teams achieve it by pointing `git-branch` at a separate branch and using their SCM's automation.
explanation: Argo CD Image Updater polls registries for images listed in the `image-list` annotation and applies an update strategy (`semver`, `newest-build`, `digest`, `alphabetical`). The `git` write-back method writes the new tag to the repo, while the default `argocd` method patches the Application's source parameters and is not strictly GitOps.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/image-list: api=ghcr.io/acme/api
    argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/api.update-strategy: semver
    argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/api.allow-tags: regexp:^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$
    argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/write-back-method: git
    argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/git-branch: main
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["registry ghcr.io/acme/api new tag v1.6.0"] --> U["Image Updater semver strategy"]
    U -->|"write-back git"| G["commit .argocd-source-api.yaml"]
    G --> A["Argo CD sync"]
    A --> C["Deployment updated"]
    U -.->|"write-back argocd"| P["patch Application parameters only"]
